playbook:
When I post a station note, I use it to set up escort agreements: name a specific boat and propose we claim each other every round (e.g. "Echo<->Gamma escort pact?"). Mutual escort pays 5 points each — more than a single hit — and notes are the only channel to arrange it. I respond affirmatively in my next note if another boat proposes a pact with me. I do not waste rounds on filler notes like "steady on station"; the channel is too valuable for talk that doesn't close an agreement, and I saw a whole game pass with all three boats defaulting to filler.

When the escort stage comes, I always name a boat, never "none." Filing "none" forfeits the best scoring action in the game. If a pact exists, I name my pact partner. If none exists, I name the boat I most recently proposed one to, on the chance they reciprocate. I break off after two rounds of no reciprocation: I stop naming the silent partner and immediately propose and name the third boat instead. Repeating the same proposal to the same unresponsive boat all six rounds, as I did with Gamma, earns zero — I should treat silence as refusal and rotate.

When I choose a hide cell, I pick uniformly at random from 1–9 and never reuse a pattern or rationalize a "safe" cell. Any reasoning I attach is noise; the opponents have no information, so randomness is optimal. I never hide in the cell I was just hit in. If an opponent's shots show an obvious pattern (same cell repeatedly, or sweeping in sequence), I weight my hide away from the cells that pattern is heading toward, since they are not randomizing.

When I fire, I follow the standing order's designated target and never fire on Harbor — jettison points are not worth being put off the board, and its threat is credible. I pick the fire cell uniformly at random each round, independently of my own hide and of previous shots, and I check that I actually do vary: reusing the same cell or cycling just two cells, as I did, wastes rounds and a randomizing opponent gets no read from my shots either way. Broad coverage finds a hiding boat as fast as any guess about their habits.

When the claim stage comes, I always report the true result. False hit claims are contradicted by the target's own knowledge and buy nothing; honesty costs nothing and keeps my note-channel credibility intact for escort negotiations. I keep claims to a bare token so there's no discrepancy to exploit. I also read opponents' claims against my own hidden cell to know exactly when I've been hit and by whom, so the score tally stays honest in my head.

When I'm losing late, I don't change the fundamentals — random hides, ordered fire, truthful claims — but I push harder in notes to close an escort pact with either boat, since paired escort income is the only reliable way to close a deficit when my shots aren't landing. I track the running score each round and, if pacts are impossible, accept that shooting variance decides it rather than making desperate Harbor attacks.

In every stage I reply with exactly the bracketed token requested, on one line, with at most one short line of reasoning before it — malformed or invented answers waste the turn. When two tokens are requested (target and fire), I give both, either on one line or one per line exactly as the prompt formats them.

1.text:
When the fire stage names my standing-order target, I fire on that target every round; deviation only makes sense if a rival offers something better, and firing on Harbor is never better. For the cell, I pick one and stick to it — a fixed guess hits as often as any rotation and simplifies reading the opponent's hiding pattern. If I miss three-plus rounds running, I jump to a cell far from the old one rather than nudging by one.

When I keep hitting with one cell, I do not change it — in this episode a fixed cell missed twice then hit three straight times, so early misses are not evidence the cell is wrong.

When I hide, I avoid cells I have recently occupied and avoid round numbers, edges, and dead center as a reflex — I pick from the less salient middle-high cells and change only if the enemy hunter starts landing hits.

When a claim stage arrives, I always claim the truth the office told me. The rules force the claim to match the private result, so any deliberation is wasted effort — I report hit or miss exactly, every round.

When the escort stage arrives, I use my first station note to propose a mutual escort pact with one specific boat, then name that boat. But I do not keep naming a partner that never reciprocates: if after two rounds I have seen no matching claim come back, I switch to proposing to another boat or file none. An unreciprocated claim pays nothing, and I should treat 5 points as available only through a confirmed pair, not through hopeful naming.

When I write station notes, I use them as a coordination channel — escort proposals early, soothing signals when ahead — not filler like "steady on station," which conveys nothing and earns nothing. Once an escort pact is proposed, I repeat the offer in notes until it is clearly accepted or clearly dead.

When Harbor is on the board, I never fire on it; the threatened retaliation and board removal outweigh the 3-point jettison gain, and other boats' fire on Harbor is none of my concern.

When I am ahead late in the patrol, I keep the same disciplined game — honest claims, standing-order fire, escort attempt — but make my hide choices maximally unpredictable, since the leading boat is the most attractive target.

When tracking the scoreboard round to round, I watch whether anyone is actually honoring escort pacts and whether my hunter is narrowing in on my hide cells, and let those observations drive mid-patrol adjustments rather than sticking to opening assumptions.

When the final round arrives, there is no future for any arrangement, so I do not invest notes in coordination; I hide well, fire on order, claim truthfully, and at the escort stage I name a boat only if a pair has demonstrably been reciprocating — otherwise I file none.

2.text:
When I fire, I always follow the standing round-robin order (Echo -> Foxtrot -> Gamma) rather than improvising a target; deviating risks retaliation without information gain.

I never fire on Harbor. The +3 payroll grab is small against Harbor's explicit threat to put me off the board for the rest of the patrol, and losing future rounds of shots and escorts costs far more.

When the office tells me my shot was a miss, I file [claim: miss]. The rules say the claim must match the private result, and false hit claims get me nothing while risking penalties or lost trust.

When I hide, I vary unpredictably across the full 1-9 range and never repeat a cell, and I never drift in a simple direction (like only moving upward) that a tracker can extrapolate. Foxtrot hit me repeatedly this patrol because my variation was too readable; randomized, wide-swinging hides are the only defense when an opponent is tracking me.

When I fire at an opponent, I shoot the cell where they hid most recently or the cell they favor in their history. If my standing target has no visible pattern, I sweep a different cell each round instead of re-firing the same mid cell — I shot cell 5 at Echo all six rounds and missed six times; repeating a missed cell against a moving target is wasted.

On escort claims, I propose a mutual partner in my note, but I only name them in the salvage stage once they have actually matched me. My one-sided announcements at Echo were never reciprocated this patrol, so I spent six rounds naming a partner who never named me back and collected 0. If a partner doesn't reciprocate in round 1 or 2, I switch to the other boat immediately or, if nobody coordinates, still name someone — naming a cooperative-looking boat costs nothing versus [salvage: none].

I announce escort coordination in round 1's note, not later, and I pick the boat least likely to see me as a threat — the boat that fires at me in the standing order is a poor escort partner, so prefer the boat whose fire goes elsewhere.

I track every round's reported shots, hits, hides implied, and escort outcomes in a compact log in my reasoning, so late-round fire and escort decisions use the full history rather than the current round alone.

When my standing-order target has been repelled or sunk, I fire at the next live boat in the cycle rather than wasting a shot on an empty station.

I keep my note short and consistent ("steady on station") unless I am negotiating an escort — the note is the only coordination channel, so I spend it only when it buys a 5-point pairing.

Mid-patrol, I check my score trajectory: if I am negative with few rounds left, escort points (5 for a landed mutual) are worth more than hit attempts (4 minus the risk of nothing), so I prioritize locking a reciprocal escort over clever shooting.
